title: 3D coordinates
description: 3D coordinates: x, y and z axes drawn in 3D (isometric), a point P moved with sliders, and dashed lines that show how
reference:
- `widget: space3d` (first used by `maths/angles/3d-coordinates`): x, y and z axes in isometric view (`size: 6`, 2 to 10)
    with a point P set by `slider x:`, `slider y:`, `slider z:` (or fixed), its path from the origin dashed. `target: 3, 2, 4`
    draws a ring Q; `box: on` draws the box from the origin to P. Values `x`, `y`, `z`, `d` (1 on the target), `v` (the box's
    volume). Use a height near 680. Checks: `"d = 1"`, `"v = 24"`.

3D coordinates: x, y and z axes drawn in 3D (isometric), a point P moved with sliders, and dashed lines that show how
far it is along each axis. Optionally a target point Q to reach, or a box with a corner at P.
  widget: space3d
  slider x: 0, 6, 2     slider y: 0, 6, 3     slider z: 0, 6, 1     (or fixed "x: 2")
  size: 6               the length of each axis (2 to 10)
  target: 3, 2, 4       a point Q (shown as a ring) to move P to
  box: on               draw the box from the origin to P (its edges are x, y and z long)
state: { scope: { vars: { x, y, z, d (1 when P is on the target), v (the box's volume x × y × z) } } }
Checks: "x = 3 and y = 2 and z = 4", "d = 1".
example:
widget: space3d
slider x: 0, 6, 0
slider y: 0, 6, 0
slider z: 0, 6, 0

title: A made-up video feed for AI in your life

reference:
- `widget: feed` (first used by `ai/ai-in-your-life/`): a made-up video feed, labelled as a model. `mode: rank`: eight

A made-up video feed for AI in your life. NOT a real app or a real recommender: a small, inspectable model
that ranks eight made-up posts by a weighted sum of signals, so students can "be the algorithm".
  widget: feed
  mode: rank | design
mode: rank    Eight posts for a made-up student, Sam. Sliders (0 to 3) set how much each signal counts: watch time,
              likes, shares and comments, from people Sam follows, matches what Sam says he wants. The feed re-sorts

          Sam follows in the top 3), w (watch-time weight), s (wants weight), p (1 when the app's goal preset is set)
mode: design  Switch app features on and off and see how long a made-up session lasts (a made-up model, labelled as

          Sam's plan)

title: A small bitmap
description: A small bitmap: a grid of pixels, each stored as numbers. Set a colour with the red, green and blue sliders (0 to
reference:
- `widget: pixels` (first used by `systems/data/colour-and-images`): a bitmap grid; sliders set a red, green, blue brush
    (0 to 255; `mode: grey` for one number) and clicking a pixel paints it. `size: 4, 4` (up to 12 × 12), `colour: 255, 0, 0`
    (the brush), `start: white | black` or rows of key letters (`wwww / wrrw / …`), `target:` rows to copy (shown small),
    `key:` extra letters (`o=255,128,0`; defaults w k r g b y), `numbers: on`, `sliders: off`. The panel counts the numbers
    the image needs. Values: `r`, `g`, `b` (brush), `p`, `q`, `s` (the last pixel painted), `m` (1 when it matches the
    target), `n` (numbers in the image), `c` (pixels changed). Checks: `"p = 255 and q = 255 and s = 0"`, `"m = 1"`.
    Compression (first used by `systems/compression/`): `mode: bw` (black or white, a Black and a White button for the
    brush), `rle: on` writes each row's run-length code beside it (bw: run lengths taking turns from white, a leading 0
    when a row starts black; otherwise count × value pairs), `show: codes` shows the target only as its codes (draw the
    picture from them), digits 0 to 9 in `start:`/`target:` are greys from black to white, and `lossy: on` (grey mode)
    shows the start picture compressed with a Tolerance slider (0 to 128; a pixel joins the run before it when within
    the tolerance), the original drawn small beside it. Extra values: `k` (numbers in the codes), `t` (tolerance), `d`
    (pixels that came back different). Checks: `"k = 8"`, `"t = 27 and d = 0"`.

A small bitmap: a grid of pixels, each stored as numbers. Set a colour with the red, green and blue sliders (0 to
255, light, not paint), then click pixels to paint them. The panel counts how many numbers the image needs.
  widget: pixels
  size: 4, 4             columns, rows (1 to 12 each)
  mode: rgb              rgb (three numbers a pixel) | grey (one number a pixel, 0 black to 255 white)
                         | bw (black or white, one number a pixel; the brush is two buttons)
  colour: 255, 0, 0      the starting brush (r, g, b; one number in grey mode)
  start: white           every pixel's starting colour: white | black, or rows of letters (see key) such as
                         start: wwww / wrrw / wrrw / wwww   (rows split by /)
  target: …              rows of letters for a picture to copy, drawn small beside the grid (checks: m = 1)
  show: codes            show the target only as its run-length codes (draw the picture from the codes)
  key: w=255,255,255 k=0,0,0 r=255,0,0 g=0,255,0 b=0,0,255 y=255,255,0, and digits 0 to 9 for greys from black (0)
                         to white (9); add more as letter=r,g,b or letter=grey
  numbers: on            show each pixel's numbers in its square (a button switches them otherwise)
  sliders: off           no sliders: the brush stays at colour: (a paint-only task)
  rle: on                run-length codes beside each row. In bw mode (CS Unplugged's form) each row is the lengths
                         of its runs, starting with white (0 first if the row starts black). Otherwise each run is a
                         pair, count × value (count × r,g,b in rgb mode), so 2 numbers a run (4 in rgb).
  lossy: on              grey mode only: no painting. The start picture is compressed with a Tolerance slider: a pixel
                         joins the run before it if it is within the tolerance of the run's value. The grid shows
                         what comes back; the original is drawn small beside it.
state: { scope: { vars: { r, g, b (the brush), p, q, s (the last pixel painted or clicked: red, green, blue),
         m (1 when the grid matches the target, else 0), n (numbers the image needs as pixels), c (pixels that are
         not the start colour), k (numbers in the run-length codes), t (tolerance), d (pixels that came back
         different from the original) } } }
Checks: "p = 255 and q = 255 and s = 0", "m = 1", "k < 20", "t > 0 and d = 0", "k <= 16".
example:
widget: pixels
size: 3, 3
colour: 0, 0, 0
start: white

title: A tiny processor
description: A tiny processor: 16 memory cells, a program counter (PC), an instruction register (IR) and an accumulator (ACC).
reference:
- `widget: cpu` (first used by `systems/logic/processor`): 16 memory cells and a processor (PC, IR, ACC); Clock tick
    (one phase of fetch, decode, execute), Whole instruction, Run, Reset. `program: LOAD 6; ADD 7; OUT; HALT` from cell 0,
    `data: 6=5, 7=3`, `edit: on` (cells are text boxes labelled `Memory 0`…; type `ADD 7` or a number, Enter), `expect:
    2, 4, 6`, `watch: 9`. Instructions are numbers (operation × 16 + address): 0 HALT, 1 LOAD, 2 ADD, 3 SUB, 4 STORE,
    5 JUMP, 6 JZ, 7 OUT; numbers wrap at 256; stops after 600 ticks. Values `p`, `a`, `t` ticks, `i` instructions, `h`
    halted, `o` last output (−1 none), `n` outputs, `x` (halted with exactly the expected outputs), `v` watched cell, `e`
    error, `q` cells typed, `f` phase.

A tiny processor: 16 memory cells, a program counter (PC), an instruction register (IR) and an accumulator (ACC).
Each clock tick is one phase: fetch (IR = memory[PC], PC + 1), decode (work out the instruction), execute (do it).
  widget: cpu
  program: LOAD 6; ADD 7; OUT; HALT     cells from 0 (instructions, or plain numbers)
  data: 6=5, 7=3                        numbers in other cells
  edit: on                              memory cells can be typed into ("ADD 7" or a number)
  expect: 8                             outputs wanted, in order (gives x)
  watch: 9                              the cell reported as v
Instructions are numbers too: code = operation × 16 + address. 0 HALT, 1 LOAD a (ACC = cell a), 2 ADD a, 3 SUB a,
4 STORE a (cell a = ACC), 5 JUMP a, 6 JZ a (jump if ACC is 0), 7 OUT (show ACC). Numbers wrap at 256 (8 bits).
state: { scope: { vars: { p (PC), a (ACC), t (clock ticks), i (instructions done), h (1 halted), o (last output, −1
         none), n (outputs), x (1 when halted and the outputs are exactly the expected ones), v (the watched cell),
         e (1 if stopped by an error or too many steps), q (cells changed by typing), f (phase: 0 fetch next,
         1 decode next, 2 execute next) } } }
Checks: "h = 1 and o = 8", "t >= 3", "x = 1", "h = 1 and v = 12".
example:
widget: cpu
data: 15=2
edit: on
expect: 2, 4, 6

title: A web document as three layers

reference:
- `widget: webdoc` (first used by `systems/web/`): a web page as content, structure and presentation, drawn in a shadow root (student HTML is cleaned: no scripts, frames or event attributes). `doc: club | messy` (the same words with headings, a list and landmarks, or faked with font, b and br), `compare: on` (Page A / Page B), `styles: plain, ocean, poster` (buttons; the first starts), `edit: css | html | both` (text boxes "Style sheet (CSS)", "Page (HTML)"), `pages: on` (two more pages of the site share the style sheet), `reader: off`. Buttons: Style sheet, Show structure (tag outlines), Screen reader (announces headings, links, lists, landmarks), Phone width. Values `o`, `e` (structure shown once), `p`, `y`, `n` styles tried, `c`/`t` CSS/HTML edits, `u` structure unchanged, `d` words unchanged, `w` looks different, `a` h1 colour changed, `f` h2 px, `g` background changed, `r`, `v`, `h` headings, `l` lists, `k` landmarks, `b` look-only tags, `x` (2+ headings, a list, no look-only tags), `j` pages heard. A web document as three layers: content (the words and pictures), structure (HTML tags that say what each part is) and presentation (CSS that says how it looks). Switch the style sheet, show the structure, hear what a screen reader reads, see it at phone width, and edit the HTML or the CSS. widget: webdoc doc: club club (tidy: headings, a list, header/nav/main/footer) | messy (the same words, styled with , and
instead of structure) compare: on Page A (club) and Page B (messy) buttons styles: plain, ocean, poster style sheet buttons (the first is the starting one) edit: none | css | html | both text boxes (labelled "Style sheet (CSS)" and "Page (HTML)") pages: on three pages of the same site share the one style sheet (small previews) reader: on | off the screen reader button (default on) state: { scope: { vars: { o (structure outlines on), p (style sheet on), y (style index, 1-based), n (styles tried), c (CSS edits), t (HTML edits), u (1 if the structure (tags) is the same as at the start), d (1 if the words are the same), w (1 if it looks different from the start), a (1 if the main heading's colour changed), f (h2 font size, px), g (1 if the page background changed), r (screen reader on), v (phone width), h (headings), l (lists), k (landmarks: header, nav, main, footer), b (presentational tags: font, center, b, u, br), x (1 when there are 2+ headings, a list and no presentational tags), j (pages heard in the screen reader, of A and B), e (1 once the structure outlines have been shown) } } }

title: Adding fractions
description: Adding fractions: two fraction bars (a/b and c/d) and the sum or difference end to end below, with every bar cut into
reference:
- `widget: fracadd` (first used by `maths/number/adding-fractions`): two fraction bars `a/b` and `c/d` (sliders or fixed
    values; bottoms 1 to 24) and their sum or difference end to end below, every bar cut into `k` parts (`slider k`, or
    `k: 12`). When `k` is a common multiple of both bottoms the parts can be counted ("1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12");
    otherwise the panel says which bar does not split. `op: + | − | ?` (? gives + and − buttons). A second whole is
    drawn only when a sum is more than 1. Values: `a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, `k`, `e` (1 when k splits both), `l` (1 when k is
    the LCM), `o` (1 or −1), `p` (parts of k in the answer), `r` (its value). Checks: `"e = 1"`, `"e = 1 and l = 1"`,
    `"o = 1 and r = 1 and (b - d)^2 > 0"` (there is no `!=`).

Adding fractions: two fraction bars (a/b and c/d) and the sum or difference end to end below, with every bar cut into
k parts, the denominator students choose. When k is a common multiple of b and d, every bar splits evenly and the
parts can be counted: 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12; otherwise the board says which bar does not split.
  widget: fracadd
  slider a: 0, 6, 1        the first fraction's top (or fixed "a: 1"); slider b for its bottom
  slider c: 0, 6, 1        the second fraction (c/d)
  slider k: 1, 24, 7       the number of equal parts to cut each whole into (or fixed "k: 12")
  op: +                    + (default), − (or -), or ? (+ and − buttons)
state: { scope: { vars: { a, b, c, d, k, e (1 when k is a common multiple of b and d), l (1 when k is the lowest),
  o (1 for +, −1 for −), p (parts of k in the answer, when e = 1), r (the answer's value) } } }
Checks: "e = 1 and k = 12", "e = 1 and l = 1", "r = 7/12" (written "abs(r - 7/12) < 0.001" is safer).
example:
widget: fracadd
a: 1
b: 3
c: 1
d: 4
slider k: 1, 24, 7

title: Arduino breadboard
description: A breadboard wired to an Arduino Uno (Engineering › Physical computing). Students move part legs between holes
reference:
- `widget: breadboard` (first used by `engineering/arduino/breadboard`): a breadboard beside an Uno's 13, 12, 9, 5V and
    GND terminals. Each numbered column's a–e holes are one strip, f–j another, and the rails (`t+3`, `t-3`, `b+3`, `b-3`)
    run the board's length. `cols: 17`, `pin: 13` (taken as HIGH), `part LED: led, c7, c8` (anode first), `resistor`,
    `wire`, `button` (Hold B1); `lock: W1, R`. Click a hole to light everything joined to it; click a leg's dot then a
    hole to move it, or use Move [leg] to [hole]. Values `l` (first LED lit), `r` (a resistor in its loop), `x` (no
    resistor), `z` (pin or 5V straight to GND), `v` (would light turned round), `y` (both legs in one strip), `q` (holes
    looked at), `m` (legs moved), `p` (button held). Ready selector `.bbsvg`.

A breadboard wired to an Arduino Uno (Engineering › Physical computing). Students move part legs between holes
and the board works out what is connected: each numbered column's five holes a–e are joined, so are f–j (not across
the gap), and each rail runs the board's length. A sketch is taken to be switching the named pin HIGH.
  widget: breadboard
  cols: 17                      columns (8 to 24)
  pin: 13                       the Uno pin the sketch switches HIGH (terminals 13, 5V and GND are on the left)
  part LED: led, a10, a11       a part: led (anode = long leg first, then cathode), resistor, wire, button
  part R: resistor, b5, b9        legs at holes (a1–j24, rails t+5 t-5 b+5 b-5) or terminals (13, 5V, GND)
  part W1: wire, 13, a5
  lock: W1, R                   parts whose legs cannot move
Click a hole to see everything joined to it; click a leg's handle, then a hole, to move it (or type a move).
state: { scope: { vars: { l (1 = the first LED lights), r (1 = a resistor is in its loop), x (1 = an LED with no
  resistor: too much current), z (1 = a short: the pin or 5V joined straight to GND), v (1 = the first LED would
  light the other way round), y (1 = both its legs in one strip), q (holes looked at), m (legs moved),
  p (1 = a button is held) } } }
example:
widget: breadboard
part W1: wire, 13, j2
part W2: wire, GND, j4
part R: resistor, i12, i15
part LED: led, h12, h13

title: Arduino Uno
description: An Arduino Uno running a small sketch (Engineering › Physical computing). Not a compiler: the sketch is turned into
reference:
- `widget: arduino` (first used by `engineering/arduino/`): an Uno running a sketch in an editor, with Upload and run,
    Stop and Reset code. Not a compiler: a C++ subset turned into JavaScript and run against a model with simulated time
    (so `delay` timings are exact). Supports `setup()`/`loop()`, own functions, int/long/float/bool/byte/const, if/else/
    for/while, pinMode, digitalWrite/Read, analogRead (0–1023 for 0–5 V), analogWrite, delay, millis, map, constrain,
    Serial.begin/print/println. Behaves like the real board for what lessons teach: a missing `;` or an undeclared name
    stops the upload (naming the line), `=` in an if assigns, HIGH without pinMode OUTPUT glows dimly (pull-up),
    `"words" + n` moves along the text, analogWrite keeps the low 8 bits and is on/off on non-PWM pins, nothing prints
    before Serial.begin. Setup: `led: 13` (or `13, 9`), `knob: A0`, `level:` (%), `button: 2`, `wave: on` (draw each LED
    pin's signal), `edit: off`, `run: on`, then the sketch as `code:` lines (indentation is rebuilt from the braces; no
    `#` lines, which the setup format reads as comments). Values `e`, `g`, `l`, `h`, `o`, `f` (ms), `t`, `s`, `m`, `w`,
    `n`, `p`, `j`, `x`, `k`, `b` (the widget's header lists them). `test: 250, on` lines (a knob reading, and the first LED
    `on` steady, `off` or `blink`) add **Run the tests**: each case runs on a fresh board for 3 s of board time with no
    waiting, and the monitor lists ✓ and ✗; values `q` (passed) and `u` (cases). Ready selector `.ardsvg`.

An Arduino Uno running a small sketch (Engineering › Physical computing). Not a compiler: the sketch is turned into
JavaScript and run against a simple model of the board, so lessons can run, change and check Arduino C++ in the
browser. Supported: setup() and loop(), your own functions, int / long / float / bool / byte / const variables,
if / else / for / while, pinMode, digitalWrite, digitalRead, analogRead, analogWrite, delay, millis, map, constrain,
Serial.begin / print / println, HIGH LOW OUTPUT INPUT INPUT_PULLUP A0–A5. Time is simulated: delay(500) is 500 ms
of board time (shown in real time), so timings are exact. Like the real board: a missing ; stops the upload, an
undeclared name is an error, = inside if assigns, "words" + n moves along the text instead of joining, analogWrite
keeps only the low 8 bits (300 acts like 44), a pin written HIGH without pinMode(pin, OUTPUT) only glows
dimly (the pull-up), analogWrite on a non-PWM pin is just on or off, and analogRead gives 0–1023 for 0–5 V.
  widget: arduino
  led: 13            an LED (with its resistor) on pin 13; up to two: led: 13, 9
  knob: A0           a potentiometer on A0 (a slider)         button: 2   a button on pin 2 (with a pull-down)
  level: 50          the knob's starting position, %          wave: on    draw each LED pin's signal (PWM)
  edit: off          the code can be run but not changed       run: on     start running as soon as it loads
  test: 250, on      a test case for Run the tests: knob reading, and the first LED on (steady), off or blink
  code: void setup() {     one line of the sketch per code: line (indentation is put back from the braces)
state: { scope: { vars: { e (1 = an error stopped it), g (1 = running), l (first LED's brightness 0–255),
  h (times the first LED came on), o and f (its last on and off times, ms of board time), t (loop() runs),
  s (setup() runs), m (1 = the first LED's pin set to OUTPUT), w (its analogWrite value, −1 if none),
  n (lines printed), p (the last printed line as a number, −1 if not a number), j (the number at the end of a last
  line that starts with words, −1 if none), x (1 = "words" + a number was printed), k (knob 0–1023), b (button held), q and u (tests passed, of how many) } } }

title: Area
description: Area: a parallelogram, triangle or rectangle on a grid of unit squares, with its base and perpendicular height marked,
reference:
- `widget: area` (first used by `maths/measurement/parallelograms`): `shape: parallelogram | triangle | rectangle` on
    a grid of unit squares, with the base and the perpendicular height (dashed, with a right-angle mark) labelled.
    Sliders or fixed values `b` (base), `h` (height) and `s` (where the top sits: a parallelogram's top-left corner or a
    triangle's apex, measured along from the base's left end; default 2, or b ÷ 2 for a triangle). The top can also be
    dragged along its line (`drag: off` stops it). When the top is past an end, the base is extended (dashed) to meet
    the height. `cut: on` adds **Cut and move** (a parallelogram rearranged into a rectangle) or **Add a turned copy**
    (a triangle doubled into a parallelogram); `cut: shown` starts that way. `slant: on` also labels the left slanted
    side. `units: cm`. Values: `b`, `h`, `s`, `a` (area), `l` (slanted side, 2 dp), `c` (1 while cut or copied), `o` (1
    when the height falls outside the base). Checks: `"c = 1"`, `"s = 0"`, `"b = 8 and a = 24"`, `"o = 1"`, `"a = 18 and s^2 > 0"`.

Area: a parallelogram, triangle or rectangle on a grid of unit squares, with its base and perpendicular height marked,
so A = bh and A = ½bh can be seen, not just used. The top (a parallelogram's top-left corner, a triangle's apex) slides
along a line parallel to the base: the area does not change. A parallelogram can be cut and the piece moved to make a
rectangle; a triangle can be doubled with a turned copy to make a parallelogram.
  widget: area
  shape: parallelogram     or triangle, rectangle
  slider b: 1, 10, 6       the base (or fixed "b: 6")
  slider h: 1, 8, 4        the perpendicular height (or fixed)
  slider s: -3, 9, 2       how far along the top sits (a parallelogram's top-left corner or a triangle's apex),
                           from the left end of the base (or fixed; default 2 for a parallelogram, b ÷ 2 for a triangle)
  cut: on                  a parallelogram's "Cut and move" button, or a triangle's "Add a turned copy";
                           "cut: shown" starts that way (pictures)
  slant: on                also label the left slanted side's length (it is not the height)
  units: cm                lengths in cm, areas in cm²
  drag: on                 the top can be dragged along its line too (default on when s has a slider)
state: { scope: { vars: { b, h, s, a (area), l (the left slanted side, 2 dp), c (1 while cut or copied),
  o (1 when the height falls outside the base, as in an obtuse triangle) } } }
Checks: "a = 24", "b = 8 and h = 3", "c = 1", "s = 0" (a right angle), "o = 1".
example:
widget: area
shape: parallelogram
b: 6
h: 4
s: 2
cut: on
units: cm

title: Area of a circle
description: Area of a circle: cut a circle into n equal pieces (sectors) and rearrange them, alternately up and down, into a
reference:
- `widget: circlearea` (first used by `maths/measurement/circle-area`): a circle (`slider r:` or `r: 3`) cut into `n` slices
    (even, 4 to 64); `cut: on` adds Rearrange the pieces (alternately up and down: nearly a rectangle πr by r) and Put the
    circle back (`cut: shown` starts rearranged); `squares: on` adds Compare with squares (the 4r² and 2r² squares and one r²).
    Values `r`, `n`, `a` (πr²), `c` (2πr), `w` (πr), `k` (1 while rearranged), `s` (1 while the squares show).

Area of a circle: cut a circle into n equal pieces (sectors) and rearrange them, alternately up and down, into a
shape that gets closer to a rectangle πr long and r high as n grows; or compare the circle with squares of side r
(it is more than 2r² and less than 4r²).
  widget: circlearea
  slider r: 1, 5, 3        the radius (or fixed "r: 3")
  slider n: 4, 32, 8, 4    how many pieces (even; or fixed "n: 8")
  cut: on                  the "Rearrange the pieces" button (and "Put the circle back"); "cut: shown" starts rearranged
  squares: on              the "Compare with squares" button; "squares: shown" starts that way
  units: cm
state: { scope: { vars: { r, n, a (πr², 2 dp), c (2πr, 2 dp), w (πr, 2 dp, the long side), k (1 while
  rearranged), s (1 while the squares show) } } }
Checks: "k = 1 and n >= 16", "r = 4", "s = 1".
example:
widget: circlearea
slider r: 0.5, 6, 1, 0.5
n: 16
units: m

title: Atoms (AC9S9U06, AC9S10U06)
description: Atoms (AC9S9U06, AC9S10U06): the nuclear atom drawn as a Bohr model, built particle by particle or chosen from the
reference:
- `widget: atom` (AC9S9U06, AC9S10U06): a Bohr model, not to scale. `mode: build` (default): + and − for
    protons, neutrons and electrons (aria-labels "Protons: more" and so on); the board names the element (1 to 20),
    gives atomic number, mass number, charge and shells (2, 8, 8, 2). `start: 6, 6, 6` (p, n, e), `target:

title: Atoms and molecules
description: Inspect molecules to distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures.
reference:

revising one idea, beside practical work, never instead of it. One tutorial per hinge node of the XY Model node files
(waypoints-kit `data/science/`); nodes whose response mode is `integration` are left to class tasks.

- **Woven strands.** Human endeavour and Inquiry have no tutorials of their own; they are woven into lessons. A lesson
  lists the ones a student genuinely practises in it as `woven: [AC9S7H03, AC9S7I05]` (descriptor codes from
  `data/curriculum/science.json`; validate checks each is in a woven strand), and the curriculum map lists those lessons on
  the descriptor's card. A predict step alone isn't Inquiry; tag only where the student does the thing (judges a claim,
  finds an anomaly, weighs impacts). Where a descriptor has no lesson, add a short `tier: typical` Elaborate step.
- **5E on the existing stages.** Science pages label the stages in 5E words, so predict-and-compare, decks and
  worksheets work unchanged: `predict` = **Engage** (one `predict` check, with `actual:`), `run` = **Explore** (a board;
  the compare box shows the prediction), `investigate` = **Explain**, `practise` = **Practise** (when the node's response
  mode is consolidation), `modify` = **Elaborate**, `info` = **Evaluate** (a `reflect` check and a revision summary).
- **`prompt:`** (step field; the Learning with AI courses): a copyable AI prompt card, text or `{ title, text }`. The page adds a Copy button and "Use an AI tool your school allows, and only if your teacher says you can". Keep the lesson doable without it (put it on an optional step), one prompt per step, and ask students to check the reply with the habit the lesson practised. General lessons keep coach prompts on recap pages only.
- **`video:`** (step field): a video hosted elsewhere, an `https://` address or `{ url, caption }`. YouTube and Vimeo links become a privacy-friendly embed, `.mp4`/`.webm` files a player, anything else a link. For teacher-made lessons (Create's student links); site lessons use recorded clips.
- **Width tiers** (any lesson, not only science): `tier: typical` or `tier: wider` on a step marks extra contexts beyond
  the minimum path. The page shows a Minimum / Typical / Wider control; `?width=` in the link sets the floor (a
  teacher's choice), students can widen but not narrow, and the default is typical. Tiered steps' checks are not
  needed to finish the lesson and are left out of course progress. Worksheets wrap them in `:::typical` / `:::wider`.
  Wider means more contexts, never harder content.
- **`sort` check, sort into groups** (any lesson; not ordering, which is `parsons`): `options:` are groups, `items:` are `[text, group]` or `[text, group, why]`; a group can
  be used many times (unlike `match`), and extra groups act as distractors. The why shows once an item is right.
- **`question` feedback** (any lesson): `feedback:` is one entry per option (text, or `null`), shown when that wrong
  option is chosen. Aim each at the misconception behind the option.
- **`board` check:** `expect: { done: true }` ticks when the science board's widget finishes its task.
- **The science board** (`playground-science/`: `engine.js` is the particle engine, `main.js` the widgets; JSXGraph).
  The starter is a `key: value` region in `boards.yml`. Widgets: `zoom` (`samples:` from ice, water, steam,
  distilled, salt, sand, air, copper), `identify` (`need:`), `build`, `syringe`, `diffusion`, `jar`, `heat`, `dissolve`,
  `bench`, `filter`, `evaporate`, `distil`, `chroma`, `box` (a model to look at), `windows` (`set: floatsink | six |
  ice | abc`, static diagrams) and `quiz` (`need:`, `options: Label=value; …`, repeated `item: text | value | why`).
  Each task's `starter` loads its own board. Nothing on the board is saved.
- **Atoms and reactions** (`atoms.js`, for Years 8–10 chemistry): molecules built from element atoms (model-kit
  colours, symbols on by default, `labels: off` hides them), moving as a gas in a box shaped to the screen with the same
  area everywhere. Particles are written `H2 x4` or `4 H2`; formulas use real element symbols (a typo is an error).
  - `widget: atoms`, `show: H2 x4, O2 x3, H2O x5`, optional `need:` (kinds to inspect; default all) and `temp:` (K).
    Students click particles (or press Inspect next particle) to see each kind's atoms, element or compound; with
    more than one kind the board names the box a mixture. Done once `need` kinds are inspected.
  - `widget: reaction`, `show:` and one or more `react: H2 + Cl2 -> 2 HCl` lines (atoms must balance, or the board
    refuses). Options: `ea:` energy a collision needs, in multiples of the average energy (default 3); `release:`
    energy given out per reaction (negative absorbs; try 0.5–1); `temp:` (default 300 K) and `temps: 150-600` for the
    slider (`slider: off` hides it); `catalyst: on` (a toggle that halves `ea`); `hold: on | off` (keep the temperature
    fixed; default on unless `release` is set, so exothermic and endothermic reactions warm or cool the gas);
    `target: HCl 10` (default: three quarters of what the first reaction can make). `goal:` is `target` (done when the
    target is reached), `react` (done at the first reaction), `compare` (done after reaching the target under two
    different conditions; a run whose temperature or catalyst changed part-way does not count) or `none`.
    The panel shows counts, the atom tally before and now, collisions and reactions, temperature and time; a yellow
    ring marks each collision that reacts. Simplifications to name for students: 2D, rigid molecules, and reactions with
    more than two reactants (CH4 + 2 O2) take the extra particles from nearby rather than in several steps.
    With about ten of each reactant, run times vary by a factor of two or so: use 15 or more for rate comparisons.
- **Cooling magma** (`crystals.js`, 8U04 node 2): `widget: cooling`. Students pick a cooling speed (Very slow, Slow,
  Fast, Very fast, Instant: each names where it happens, from deep underground to lava quenched in seconds), press
  Cool the magma and watch crystals start and grow; each finished run adds a row (crystals, average and largest size,
  glass). Typical results: very slow, about 5 crystals of 60 particles (like granite); fast, about 23 of 14 (like
  basalt); instant, mostly glass (like obsidian). `rates: 1, 3, 5` offers only some speeds; `goal: compare` (default:
  done after two different speeds) or `none`. `steps: 6` takes six cooling steps per frame (1 to 10): the same result in a sixth of the time. Clips use it, because the recorder plays only about 7 frames a second. Name for students: real granite and basalt also differ in what they are
  made of; the model shows only the effect of cooling speed.
- **Heat transfer** (`convection.js`): `widget: convection`. Particles are coloured blue (cool) to red (hot).
  - Default (a liquid heated from below, 9U04 node 1): a ringed particle and its trail; click another, or press Follow
    another particle. `goal: loop` (default): done when the followed particle rises, crosses the top and sinks again
    (usually 6–20 s). Heat: on/off toggle.
  - `preset: mantle` (8U03 node 2): the same current labelled as the mantle, with two plates on top that move apart
    above the rising current.
  - `mode: solid`: a bar heated at one end (conduction): the particles vibrate in place, warmer ones harder, and the
    panel shows the temperature of each quarter. `goal: spread` (default): done when the far end warms.
  Name for students: in the model hot particles are pushed up directly; in a real fluid the warm part rises because
  it has spread out (less dense).
- **Natural selection** (`selection.js`, 10U02 n1, n2): `widget: selection`. Beetles on pale (`ground: light`) or
  dark ground, colour from 0 (pale) to 1 (dark). `hunter: student` (click beetles to eat half) or `birds` (they find
  beetles that contrast with the ground more often, with some luck); then Survivors breed (offspring get the parents'
  average plus a small random change). Bar charts compare the start with the latest generation. `change: on` adds a
  button that darkens the ground (after a bushfire). `goal: generations` (default; done after `need`, default 4) or
  `measure` (no hunting: click beetles to measure; done after `need`, default 20). `n` (40), `mean` (0.5).
- Boards with hundreds of particles (cooling, convection) draw on a canvas layer over the board (`SCI.dots`), because
  SVG points cannot move that many each frame. After changing any engine, run `node tools/check-engines.mjs`.
- **Explain it to me** (science on the shared board): as for maths, `explainClip` runs a board setup (`query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain" }`) and `explainPicture` draws one (`{ ref: boards.yml#explain-pic, caption: … }`). Pictures need a drawn board (not the key widget); on the science board the picture is a moment 1.8 s after the widget starts, so choose setups that read well early (a jar starts as a gas, a syringe as wax).
- **Science pathways:** `content/science/index.md` lists Chemistry (built), Biology, Physics and Earth and space.
example:
widget: atoms
show: N2 x1, O2 x1, Ar x1, N2 x7, O2 x2

title: Balance scale
description: Balance scale: an equation as a balance, in two modes.
reference:
- `widget: balance` with `left:` and `right:` (one variable). `mode: try` (default): a slider for x; the scale tips
    and shows each side worked out. `mode: solve`: take blocks or bags of x from both sides, or share both sides into
    equal groups; the scale stays level, the steps are written as algebra, and the answer is checked in the first
    equation. Both sides must be whole-number bags and blocks (such as `2x + 3`).

Balance scale: an equation as a balance, in two modes.
  widget: balance
  left: 2x + 3, right: 11   each side an expression in one variable
  mode: try               (default) change x with a slider and watch the scale
  mode: solve             do the same to both sides until x is alone; the scale stays level throughout
  min, max, start, step   the slider's whole-number range (try mode)
  var: x                  (default x)
state (try):   { x, left, right, balanced, scope }      state (solve): { solved, steps, x, scope }
example:
widget: balance
mode: solve
left: 2x + 3
right: 11

title: Balancing chemical equations (AC9S9U07 node 4)
description: Balancing chemical equations (AC9S9U07 node 4): change only the coefficients (the big numbers in front) until every
reference:
- `widget: equation` (AC9S9U07 n4): `equation: CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O` (symbols and subscripts, no brackets, 2 to 5
    substances, at most 9 atoms each). + and − change only the coefficients (aria-labels "CH4: more" and so on, 1 to
    6); each molecule is drawn, with an atom tally per element. `start: 1, 2, 1, 2`. Values: `b` 1 while balanced,
    `l` 1 while balanced with the smallest whole numbers (check with `when: "l = 1"`), `c` changes, `m` largest
    coefficient.
  - Each task's `starter` loads its own board when the task is opened. Work is saved in the browser per step;
    `?fresh=1` on the board's address starts from the setup and saves nothing (slides on a shared projector).
  - The board's old address, `_playground-maths/`, forwards to it with the same parameters, so embeds keep working
    (the embedding contract is in the project notes).
- **Maths cards** (`snippets/maths.json`, for the course named by its `course:`): the words and methods of the course,
  one card each, with `label`, `code` (TeX, shown typeset), `hint` (may use `$...$`), `unit` (the unit whose cheat sheet
  lists it) and optionally `board` (a board setup, drawn as the card's picture by `npm run render`) with `shows` (its
  caption). They make the course's Reference page (`<course>/reference/`, with search), the student print sheets, and
  the teacher cheat sheets (A4 and Markdown for Prepare). Validate checks the maths parses and the unit exists.
- **Progression nodes:** every maths lesson names the node it teaches, `node: AC9M7A01 n2` (a list if it teaches
  more than one), from the curriculum data in `data/curriculum/maths.json` (imported from Waypoints Kit by `tools/import-curriculum.mjs`). Validate warns
  when a prerequisite is not taught by an earlier lesson: the node before it in the same descriptor, or for node 1 the
  descriptors named in its prior knowledge (all their nodes), plus anything in `uses: [AC9M7N07]` (a descriptor or
  node the lesson relies on that the data does not name, found by reading the lesson). Earlier means a lower `order`
  in the course, or a course it comes `after:` in `content/maths/index.md`. Prerequisites from an earlier year count
  as taught in class. Otherwise teach it earlier, or list it in `assumes:` (taught in class) and, where it matters,
  check it with a short retrieval question at the start or in Practise. `npm run nodes` prints the map;
  `npm run check-nodes` tests the check. Related standards are not prerequisites.
- **Maths pathways:** `content/maths/index.md` lists pathways like `code/index.md`, with planned courses as "Coming later".

Balancing chemical equations (AC9S9U07 node 4): change only the coefficients (the big numbers in front) until every
kind of atom is the same on both sides. The formulas themselves (the subscripts) are fixed: changing one would make
a different substance. Each molecule is drawn as balls, so the tally can be counted, not just computed.
  widget: equation
  equation: H2 + O2 -> H2O        formulas with element symbols and subscripts (no brackets); 2 to 5 substances
  start: 1, 1, 1                   starting coefficients (default all 1)
state: { scope: { vars: { b 1 while balanced, l 1 while balanced with the smallest whole numbers, c changes made,
  m most molecules of any one substance } } }
example:
widget: equation
equation: H2 + O2 -> H2O

title: Binary cards (after CS Unplugged's dot cards)
description: Binary cards (after CS Unplugged's dot cards): a row of cards, each worth double the one on its right (…8, 4, 2, 1),
reference:
- `widget: bits` (first used by `systems/data/binary-numbers` and `binary-patterns`): binary cards after CS Unplugged,
    each worth double the one on its right and drawn as that many dots (a number from 64 up); click a card to turn it
    face up (1) or down (0). `bits: 4` (1 to 8), `n: 11` or `start: 1011` (the starting pattern), `number: off` hides
    the sum and the number, `count: on` adds − 1 and + 1 (past the largest it overflows to 0), `grow: on` adds Add a card
    and Take away a card (1 to 8), `lock: on` makes the cards a pattern to read. Values: `n` (the number), `c` (cards
    face up), `b` (cards), `m` (largest, 2^b − 1), `o` (1 after an overflow). Checks: `"n = 11 and c = 3"`, `"o = 1"`,
    `"b = 6 and n = 39"`.

Binary cards (after CS Unplugged's dot cards): a row of cards, each worth double the one on its right (…8, 4, 2, 1),
shown as that many dots. A card face up is a 1, face down a 0; the number is the sum of the cards face up.
  widget: bits
  bits: 4            how many cards (1 to 8)
  n: 11              the starting number (or start: 1011, the starting pattern in binary)
  number: off        hide the sum and the number (students work it out); the 1s and 0s still show
  count: on          + 1 and − 1 buttons: counting past the largest number wraps round to 0 (overflow)
  grow: on           Add a card and Take away a card (1 to 8 cards)
  lock: on           the cards cannot be flipped (a pattern to read)
state: { scope: { vars: { n (the number), c (cards face up), b (cards), m (the largest number, 2^b − 1),
         o (1 once the count has wrapped round past the largest number, else 0) } } }
Checks: "n = 11", "n = 28 and c = 3", "b = 6 and n = 39", "o = 1". (Board variables are single letters.)

title: Chance

    blue 1` for spinner sector sizes or bag counters, drawn with replacement). Run 1, 10, 100 and 1000 buttons; a tally
    (count, relative frequency, probability, expected count) and a graph of the relative frequency of `watch:` (default

    hides the device too (a mystery to estimate); `seed: 7` fixes the randomness (pictures, clips); `start: 20` runs that
    many first. Values: `t` (trials), `c` (count of the watched outcome), `f` (its relative frequency), `p` (its

Chance: a coin, a dice, a spinner or a bag of counters. Students run 1, 10, 100 or 1000 trials and watch the tally,

  widget: chance
  device: coin | dice | spinner | bag

title: Changing motion (Engineering › Linkages and cams)

  `data/curriculum/science.json`; validate checks each is in a woven strand), and the curriculum map lists those lessons on

  needed to finish the lesson and are left out of course progress. Worksheets wrap them in `:::typical` / `:::wider`.

  `bench`, `filter`, `evaporate`, `distil`, `chroma`, `box` (a model to look at), `windows` (`set: floatsink | six |
  ice | abc`, static diagrams) and `quiz` (`need:`, `options: Label=value; …`, repeated `item: text | value | why`).
  Each task's `starter` loads its own board. Nothing on the board is saved.
- **Atoms and reactions** (`atoms.js`, for Years 8–10 chemistry): molecules built from element atoms (model-kit
  colours, symbols on by default, `labels: off` hides them), moving as a gas in a box shaped to the screen with the same
  area everywhere. Particles are written `H2 x4` or `4 H2`; formulas use real element symbols (a typo is an error).

  average plus a small random change). Bar charts compare the start with the latest generation. `change: on` adds a
  button that darkens the ground (after a bushfire). `goal: generations` (default; done after `need`, default 4) or
  `measure` (no hunting: click beetles to measure; done after `need`, default 20). `n` (40), `mean` (0.5).

  SVG points cannot move that many each frame. After changing any engine, run `node tools/check-engines.mjs`.
- **Explain it to me** (science on the shared board): as for maths, `explainClip` runs a board setup (`query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain" }`) and `explainPicture` draws one (`{ ref: boards.yml#explain-pic, caption: … }`). Pictures need a drawn board (not the key widget); on the science board the picture is a moment 1.8 s after the widget starts, so choose setups that read well early (a jar starts as a gas, a syringe as wax).

title: Circuits on a micro
description: Circuits on a micro:bit's pins (Engineering › Physical computing): a simple model, not a full circuit simulator.
reference:
- `widget: circuit` (first used by `engineering/circuits/`): parts wired to a micro:bit's pins, from a simple stated
    model (pin 3.3 V, LED drops 2 V and is damaged above 20 mA, analog read 0–1023 for 0–3.3 V). `mode: led`: pin 0 →
    resistor → LED → GND; `resistor:` (ohms, 0 = none), `place: after`, `output: off`, `gnd: off`, `turned: on`, and
    controls `pinbtn: on`, `unclip: on`, `choose: on` (a resistor list), `quick: 0, 220, 1000` (a button each, named
    "Use a 1 kΩ resistor" / "Take the resistor out"), `move: on`, `flip: on`; `numbers: off` hides the current. Values `k`
    (complete loop), `o`, `i` (mA), `r`, `b` (resistor before the LED), `f` (LED turned round), `w`, `c` (pin and GND wires
    unclipped), `l` (lit), `x` (over 20 mA). `mode: button`: 3V → button → pin 0 with a 10 kΩ pull-down (`pulldown: off`,
    `toggle: on`); Hold the button (pointer or Space); the micro:bit shows a heart while pin 0 reads 1, and a floating pin
    reads at random; values `p`, `v`, `n` (presses), `d`, `z` (floating seen). `mode: sensor`: `sensor: pot | light` in a
    divider into pin 0, `level:` (%), a slider; `night: on` lights the display below `threshold:` (`threshold: edit` adds a
    slider), `volts: off`, `numbers: off`; values `a` (reading), `u` (volts), `s` (%), `t`, `l`. Ready selector `.cksvg`.

  widget: circuit
  mode: led | button | sensor
mode: led — pin 0 → resistor → LED → GND (or the resistor after the LED)
  output: on        pin 0 starts on (off: starts off)       pinbtn: on   a "Pin 0 on/off" button
  resistor: 220     ohms (0 = no resistor)                  choose: on   pick the resistor
  quick: 0, 220, 1000   a button for each resistor (0 = No resistor)
  place: before     resistor before or after the LED         move: on     a button to move it
  unclip: on        buttons to unclip and clip the two wires  gnd: off     the GND wire starts unclipped

  turned: on        the LED starts the wrong way round
  values: k (1 = a complete loop), o (pin on), i (current, mA), r (ohms), b (1 = resistor before the LED),

  values: p (1 = held), v (pin 0 reads), n (presses), d (1 = pull-down fitted), z (1 = floating readings seen)

title: Classifier
description: Classifier: test an image model that students trained in Teachable Machine on a fixed test set, and optionally send
reference:
- `widget: classifier` (AI; first used by `code/microbit-computer`): students train an image model in Teachable
    Machine, export it with **Upload my model** and paste the link; the board tests it on a fixed set of photos.
    - `testset: recycling` (photos and labels in `playground-board/media/classifier/<name>/test.json`; the recycling set
      is made from TrashNet by `tools/classifier/make-recycling-set.py`, which also writes the two training zips),
      `groups: plain, messy` (which groups to test; default all), `classes: Paper, Plastic` (expected labels; default
      the set's), `model: ask` (default; the last model a student loaded fills in) or a link or a folder on this site,
      `webcam: on` (live preview, not checked).
    - `serial: on`: a **Connect a micro:bit** button (Web Serial, 115200 baud; Chrome or Edge). Clicking a test photo
      sends its predicted label as a line; the webcam sends a label once it holds `threshold:` (default 0.8) for 300 ms
      and differs from the last one sent. Lines the micro:bit sends back are shown; `name:number` lines (MakeCode's
      **serial write value**) become values.
    - Values for `when:` checks (every name has an underscore): `acc_all`, `acc_<group>` (0 to 1), `n_correct`,
      `n_total`, `n_classes`, `has_<label>` (1 or 0), and with serial `n_sent`, `n_replies`, `in_<name>`. Examples:
      `"acc_messy >= 0.75"`, `"has_neither = 1 and acc_neither >= 0.75"`, `"n_sent >= 3"`. Training is not checked;
      the model it makes is. The Teachable Machine library and TensorFlow.js load only when this widget is used.
    - Leave out `testset:` for a webcam-only board (driving a robot): then `classes:` names the expected labels.
      `threshold Go: 0.95` gives one label its own threshold; `unsure: on` sends **Unsure** when no label holds its
      threshold; `repeat: 1` resends the current label every second (a heartbeat for a robot's watchdog). Extra values:
      `sent_<label>` (times sent, including `sent_unsure`). The webcam is mirrored, as in Teachable Machine.
    - `testset: own`: students add **their own test photos** on the board (a class, a group name such as desk or
      dim, then the photos), shrunk to 224 px and kept in this browser only (`wp-classifier-own`), shared by every
      `testset: own` board on the site and kept in step across a lesson's boards. With `classes:` the class is a
      list; without it students type it. Extra values: `n_photos`, `n_groups`, `photos_<label>`, and `acc_min` (the
      weakest group's accuracy) once a model has run.

Classifier: test an image model that students trained in Teachable Machine on a fixed test set, and optionally send
its predictions to a micro:bit over USB (Web Serial).
  widget: classifier
  testset: recycling          the test set in media/classifier/<name>/test.json (images with a label and a group);
                              leave it out for a webcam-only board (driving a micro:bit or robot); "own" for the
                              students' own test photos (added on the board by class and group, kept in this browser
                              and shared by every board on the site that uses testset: own)
  model: ask                  students paste their shareable link (default); or a link or a path to a model folder
                              (relative to the board, e.g. media/classifier/recycling/demo/) for a demo or fallback
  classes: Paper, Plastic     the labels the test set expects (default: the test set's classes)
  groups: plain, messy        which groups to test (default all, in the test set's order)
  webcam: on                  a live webcam preview with the top label (not checked)
  serial: on                  "Connect a micro:bit": sends the top webcam label (or a clicked test image's label)
                              as a line of text, and reads lines back
  threshold: 0.8              confidence needed before the webcam sends a label (default 0.8)
  threshold Go: 0.95          a different threshold for one label (a costly mistake needs more confidence)
  unsure: on                  with serial, send "Unsure" when no label holds its threshold (so a robot can stop)
  repeat: 1                   with serial, send the current label again every so many seconds, so a robot's watchdog
                              can tell the board is still there (default: send only when the label changes)
state: { scope: { vars }, model, loaded, labels }. vars (every name has an underscore, so checks can use them):
  acc_all, acc_<group> (0-1), n_correct, n_total, n_classes, has_<label> (1 or 0; lower case, spaces as _),
  with serial: n_sent, n_replies, sent_<label> (times each label was sent, including sent_unsure), and in_<key>
  for each "key:number" line the micro:bit sent (dist:23 -> in_dist). With testset: own, also n_photos, n_groups,
  photos_<label> (photos of each class), and acc_min (the lowest group's accuracy) once a model has run. Without a test set, only n_classes, has_<label>
  and the serial values.
The Teachable Machine library and TensorFlow.js (the versions its export uses) load only when this widget is used.

title: Composite and irregular shapes
description: Composite and irregular shapes: area and perimeter on a grid of unit squares.
reference:
- `widget: composite` (first used by `maths/measurement/composite-shapes`, `irregular-shapes`): `mode: shape` draws a polygon
    (`corners: 0,0; a,0; a,3; 3,3; 3,6; 0,6`, numbers or slider letters, `slider a: 4, 10, 8`) on a unit grid with its side
    lengths (`hide: 3, 4` writes ? on those sides, counted from corner 1); `split: on` adds Cut across, Cut up and down, Take
    away from a rectangle and No cuts, which name each piece (rectangle, triangle, trapezium) and its area. Values `A`, `P`,
    `k` (0 none, 1 across, 2 up and down, 3 take away), `n` (pieces) and the slider letters. `mode: estimate` puts an irregular
    shape (`blob: lake | leaf | island`, `size: 8`) on a grid: Count the squares (full green, part orange), Finer grid and
    Coarser grid (1, 0.5, 0.25), and `slider n:` straight pieces round the edge for the perimeter. Values `g`, `f`, `p`, `e`
    (full + half the part, times one square), `t` (measured area), `c` (1 once counted), `n`, `l` (pieces' length), `m`
    (measured perimeter); the measured values show on the finest grid. Checks: `"k = 3 and A = 60"`, `"c = 1 and g = 0.25"`.

title: Congruence tests
description: Congruence tests: give some sides and angles, and the board draws every triangle that has them. If the parts allow
reference:

    drawing every triangle they allow (none, one, or two for SSA). `test: SSS | SAS | ASA | AAS | RHS | SSA | choose`
    (`choose` adds a "Give SSS" button for each). Parts are sliders or fixed values, sides `p`, `q`, `r` and angles `s`, `t`
    (defaults: sides 1 to 12 in halves, angles 10° to 170° in 5s), named by the test: SSS AB, AC, BC; SAS AB, AC, angle A;
    ASA AB, angles A, B; AAS BC (opposite A), angles A, B; RHS AB and hypotenuse BC = `r`; SSA AB, BC, angle A. Values `n`
    (0, 1 or 2 triangles), `k` (1 if the test always fixes the triangle, 0 for SSA), `p`, `q`, `r`, `s`, `t`. Sliders say
    "Make side q smaller", "Make angle s bigger". Checks: `"n = 2"`, `"p = 6 and r = 10"`.

Congruence tests: give some sides and angles, and the board draws every triangle that has them. If the parts allow
only one triangle, any two triangles with those parts are congruent (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS); SSA can allow two.
  widget: congruence
  test: SSS | SAS | ASA | AAS | RHS | SSA | choose     which parts are given ("choose" adds a button for each)
  sliders (any can be fixed, such as "p: 6"):
    sides p, q, r: 1 to 12 (step 0.5)      angles s, t: 10 to 170 (step 5)
    SSS: AB = p, AC = q, BC = r                 SAS: AB = p, AC = q, angle A = s (between them)
    ASA: AB = p, angle A = s, angle B = t       AAS: BC = p (opposite A), angle A = s, angle B = t
    RHS: angle A = 90°, BC = r (hypotenuse), AB = p    SSA: AB = p, BC = q, angle A = s (not between them)
state: { scope: { vars: { n (how many different triangles: 0, 1 or 2), k (1 if this test always fixes the triangle),
  p, q, r, s, t } } }
Checks: "n = 2", "n = 1 and k = 1", "n = 0".

title: Coordination and control

    (`n` tried). `mode: build`: students choose the receptor, command centre and effector from menus; a wrong one names
    the first wrong step (`c` built, `need` default 3). `mode: race`: a nerve and a hormone response to one fright on

title: Dichotomous key
description: Dichotomous key: students identify unnamed specimens by answering the key's yes/no questions, one step at a time.
reference:
- `widget: key` (a dichotomous key): `step A: Does it have a backbone? | B | D` (a question, then where yes and no
    lead: a step letter or an answer; the first step is the start) and `specimen: Kookaburra | Has feathers and a beak.`
    (the key's answer, what students see, and optionally a third part naming it when the answer is a group:
    `Plant | Green leaves… | Gum tree`). Specimens are anonymous until the key names them; a wrong answer points to
    the first step where the path went wrong. `need: 5`. Values: `n` identified, `k` specimens, `e` wrong.

title: Diffusion
description: Watch two substances mix through particle motion.
reference:
A lesson with `language: science` (see `content/science/chemistry/`) is a short concept tutorial for introducing or
revising one idea, beside practical work, never instead of it. One tutorial per hinge node of the XY Model node files
(waypoints-kit `data/science/`); nodes whose response mode is `integration` are left to class tasks.

- **Woven strands.** Human endeavour and Inquiry have no tutorials of their own; they are woven into lessons. A lesson
  lists the ones a student genuinely practises in it as `woven: [AC9S7H03, AC9S7I05]` (descriptor codes from
  `data/curriculum/science.json`; validate checks each is in a woven strand), and the curriculum map lists those lessons on
  the descriptor's card. A predict step alone isn't Inquiry; tag only where the student does the thing (judges a claim,
  finds an anomaly, weighs impacts). Where a descriptor has no lesson, add a short `tier: typical` Elaborate step.
- **5E on the existing stages.** Science pages label the stages in 5E words, so predict-and-compare, decks and
  worksheets work unchanged: `predict` = **Engage** (one `predict` check, with `actual:`), `run` = **Explore** (a board;
  the compare box shows the prediction), `investigate` = **Explain**, `practise` = **Practise** (when the node's response
  mode is consolidation), `modify` = **Elaborate**, `info` = **Evaluate** (a `reflect` check and a revision summary).
- **`prompt:`** (step field; the Learning with AI courses): a copyable AI prompt card, text or `{ title, text }`. The page adds a Copy button and "Use an AI tool your school allows, and only if your teacher says you can". Keep the lesson doable without it (put it on an optional step), one prompt per step, and ask students to check the reply with the habit the lesson practised. General lessons keep coach prompts on recap pages only.
- **`video:`** (step field): a video hosted elsewhere, an `https://` address or `{ url, caption }`. YouTube and Vimeo links become a privacy-friendly embed, `.mp4`/`.webm` files a player, anything else a link. For teacher-made lessons (Create's student links); site lessons use recorded clips.
- **Width tiers** (any lesson, not only science): `tier: typical` or `tier: wider` on a step marks extra contexts beyond
  the minimum path. The page shows a Minimum / Typical / Wider control; `?width=` in the link sets the floor (a
  teacher's choice), students can widen but not narrow, and the default is typical. Tiered steps' checks are not
  needed to finish the lesson and are left out of course progress. Worksheets wrap them in `:::typical` / `:::wider`.
  Wider means more contexts, never harder content.
- **`sort` check, sort into groups** (any lesson; not ordering, which is `parsons`): `options:` are groups, `items:` are `[text, group]` or `[text, group, why]`; a group can
  be used many times (unlike `match`), and extra groups act as distractors. The why shows once an item is right.
- **`question` feedback** (any lesson): `feedback:` is one entry per option (text, or `null`), shown when that wrong
  option is chosen. Aim each at the misconception behind the option.
- **`board` check:** `expect: { done: true }` ticks when the science board's widget finishes its task.
- **The science board** (`playground-science/`: `engine.js` is the particle engine, `main.js` the widgets; JSXGraph).
  The starter is a `key: value` region in `boards.yml`. Widgets: `zoom` (`samples:` from ice, water, steam,
  distilled, salt, sand, air, copper), `identify` (`need:`), `build`, `syringe`, `diffusion`, `jar`, `heat`, `dissolve`,
  `bench`, `filter`, `evaporate`, `distil`, `chroma`, `box` (a model to look at), `windows` (`set: floatsink | six |
  ice | abc`, static diagrams) and `quiz` (`need:`, `options: Label=value; …`, repeated `item: text | value | why`).
  Each task's `starter` loads its own board. Nothing on the board is saved.
- **Atoms and reactions** (`atoms.js`, for Years 8–10 chemistry): molecules built from element atoms (model-kit
  colours, symbols on by default, `labels: off` hides them), moving as a gas in a box shaped to the screen with the same
  area everywhere. Particles are written `H2 x4` or `4 H2`; formulas use real element symbols (a typo is an error).
  - `widget: atoms`, `show: H2 x4, O2 x3, H2O x5`, optional `need:` (kinds to inspect; default all) and `temp:` (K).
    Students click particles (or press Inspect next particle) to see each kind's atoms, element or compound; with
    more than one kind the board names the box a mixture. Done once `need` kinds are inspected.
  - `widget: reaction`, `show:` and one or more `react: H2 + Cl2 -> 2 HCl` lines (atoms must balance, or the board
    refuses). Options: `ea:` energy a collision needs, in multiples of the average energy (default 3); `release:`
    energy given out per reaction (negative absorbs; try 0.5–1); `temp:` (default 300 K) and `temps: 150-600` for the
    slider (`slider: off` hides it); `catalyst: on` (a toggle that halves `ea`); `hold: on | off` (keep the temperature
    fixed; default on unless `release` is set, so exothermic and endothermic reactions warm or cool the gas);
    `target: HCl 10` (default: three quarters of what the first reaction can make). `goal:` is `target` (done when the
    target is reached), `react` (done at the first reaction), `compare` (done after reaching the target under two
    different conditions; a run whose temperature or catalyst changed part-way does not count) or `none`.
    The panel shows counts, the atom tally before and now, collisions and reactions, temperature and time; a yellow
    ring marks each collision that reacts. Simplifications to name for students: 2D, rigid molecules, and reactions with
    more than two reactants (CH4 + 2 O2) take the extra particles from nearby rather than in several steps.
    With about ten of each reactant, run times vary by a factor of two or so: use 15 or more for rate comparisons.
- **Cooling magma** (`crystals.js`, 8U04 node 2): `widget: cooling`. Students pick a cooling speed (Very slow, Slow,
  Fast, Very fast, Instant: each names where it happens, from deep underground to lava quenched in seconds), press
  Cool the magma and watch crystals start and grow; each finished run adds a row (crystals, average and largest size,
  glass). Typical results: very slow, about 5 crystals of 60 particles (like granite); fast, about 23 of 14 (like
  basalt); instant, mostly glass (like obsidian). `rates: 1, 3, 5` offers only some speeds; `goal: compare` (default:
  done after two different speeds) or `none`. `steps: 6` takes six cooling steps per frame (1 to 10): the same result in a sixth of the time. Clips use it, because the recorder plays only about 7 frames a second. Name for students: real granite and basalt also differ in what they are
  made of; the model shows only the effect of cooling speed.
- **Heat transfer** (`convection.js`): `widget: convection`. Particles are coloured blue (cool) to red (hot).
  - Default (a liquid heated from below, 9U04 node 1): a ringed particle and its trail; click another, or press Follow
    another particle. `goal: loop` (default): done when the followed particle rises, crosses the top and sinks again
    (usually 6–20 s). Heat: on/off toggle.
  - `preset: mantle` (8U03 node 2): the same current labelled as the mantle, with two plates on top that move apart
    above the rising current.
  - `mode: solid`: a bar heated at one end (conduction): the particles vibrate in place, warmer ones harder, and the
    panel shows the temperature of each quarter. `goal: spread` (default): done when the far end warms.
  Name for students: in the model hot particles are pushed up directly; in a real fluid the warm part rises because
  it has spread out (less dense).
- **Natural selection** (`selection.js`, 10U02 n1, n2): `widget: selection`. Beetles on pale (`ground: light`) or
  dark ground, colour from 0 (pale) to 1 (dark). `hunter: student` (click beetles to eat half) or `birds` (they find
  beetles that contrast with the ground more often, with some luck); then Survivors breed (offspring get the parents'
  average plus a small random change). Bar charts compare the start with the latest generation. `change: on` adds a
  button that darkens the ground (after a bushfire). `goal: generations` (default; done after `need`, default 4) or
  `measure` (no hunting: click beetles to measure; done after `need`, default 20). `n` (40), `mean` (0.5).
- Boards with hundreds of particles (cooling, convection) draw on a canvas layer over the board (`SCI.dots`), because
  SVG points cannot move that many each frame. After changing any engine, run `node tools/check-engines.mjs`.
- **Explain it to me** (science on the shared board): as for maths, `explainClip` runs a board setup (`query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain" }`) and `explainPicture` draws one (`{ ref: boards.yml#explain-pic, caption: … }`). Pictures need a drawn board (not the key widget); on the science board the picture is a moment 1.8 s after the widget starts, so choose setups that read well early (a jar starts as a gas, a syringe as wax).
- **Science pathways:** `content/science/index.md` lists Chemistry (built), Biology, Physics and Earth and space.

    Students click particles (or press Inspect next particle) to see each kind's atoms, element or compound; with
    more than one kind the board names the box a mixture. Done once `need` kinds are inspected.
  - `widget: reaction`, `show:` and one or more `react: H2 + Cl2 -> 2 HCl` lines (atoms must balance, or the board
    refuses). Options: `ea:` energy a collision needs, in multiples of the average energy (default 3); `release:`
    energy given out per reaction (negative absorbs; try 0.5–1); `temp:` (default 300 K) and `temps: 150-600` for the
    slider (`slider: off` hides it); `catalyst: on` (a toggle that halves `ea`); `hold: on | off` (keep the temperature
    fixed; default on unless `release` is set, so exothermic and endothermic reactions warm or cool the gas);
    `target: HCl 10` (default: three quarters of what the first reaction can make). `goal:` is `target` (done when the
    target is reached), `react` (done at the first reaction), `compare` (done after reaching the target under two
    different conditions; a run whose temperature or catalyst changed part-way does not count) or `none`.
    The panel shows counts, the atom tally before and now, collisions and reactions, temperature and time; a yellow
    ring marks each collision that reacts. Simplifications to name for students: 2D, rigid molecules, and reactions with
    more than two reactants (CH4 + 2 O2) take the extra particles from nearby rather than in several steps.
    With about ten of each reactant, run times vary by a factor of two or so: use 15 or more for rate comparisons.
- **Cooling magma** (`crystals.js`, 8U04 node 2): `widget: cooling`. Students pick a cooling speed (Very slow, Slow,
  Fast, Very fast, Instant: each names where it happens, from deep underground to lava quenched in seconds), press
  Cool the magma and watch crystals start and grow; each finished run adds a row (crystals, average and largest size,
  glass). Typical results: very slow, about 5 crystals of 60 particles (like granite); fast, about 23 of 14 (like
  basalt); instant, mostly glass (like obsidian). `rates: 1, 3, 5` offers only some speeds; `goal: compare` (default:
  done after two different speeds) or `none`. `steps: 6` takes six cooling steps per frame (1 to 10): the same result in a sixth of the time. Clips use it, because the recorder plays only about 7 frames a second. Name for students: real granite and basalt also differ in what they are
  made of; the model shows only the effect of cooling speed.
- **Heat transfer** (`convection.js`): `widget: convection`. Particles are coloured blue (cool) to red (hot).
  - Default (a liquid heated from below, 9U04 node 1): a ringed particle and its trail; click another, or press Follow
    another particle. `goal: loop` (default): done when the followed particle rises, crosses the top and sinks again
    (usually 6–20 s). Heat: on/off toggle.
  - `preset: mantle` (8U03 node 2): the same current labelled as the mantle, with two plates on top that move apart
    above the rising current.
  - `mode: solid`: a bar heated at one end (conduction): the particles vibrate in place, warmer ones harder, and the
    panel shows the temperature of each quarter. `goal: spread` (default): done when the far end warms.
  Name for students: in the model hot particles are pushed up directly; in a real fluid the warm part rises because
  it has spread out (less dense).
- **Natural selection** (`selection.js`, 10U02 n1, n2): `widget: selection`. Beetles on pale (`ground: light`) or
  dark ground, colour from 0 (pale) to 1 (dark). `hunter: student` (click beetles to eat half) or `birds` (they find
  beetles that contrast with the ground more often, with some luck); then Survivors breed (offspring get the parents'
  average plus a small random change). Bar charts compare the start with the latest generation. `change: on` adds a
  button that darkens the ground (after a bushfire). `goal: generations` (default; done after `need`, default 4) or
  `measure` (no hunting: click beetles to measure; done after `need`, default 20). `n` (40), `mean` (0.5).
- Boards with hundreds of particles (cooling, convection) draw on a canvas layer over the board (`SCI.dots`), because
  SVG points cannot move that many each frame. After changing any engine, run `node tools/check-engines.mjs`.
- **Explain it to me** (science on the shared board): as for maths, `explainClip` runs a board setup (`query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain" }`) and `explainPicture` draws one (`{ ref: boards.yml#explain-pic, caption: … }`). Pictures need a drawn board (not the key widget); on the science board the picture is a moment 1.8 s after the widget starts, so choose setups that read well early (a jar starts as a gas, a syringe as wax).
- **Science pathways:** `content/science/index.md` lists Chemistry (built), Biology, Physics and Earth and space.

title: Encoding and encryption
description: Encoding is not encryption. A message written as binary, hex or base64 looks scrambled, but the rule is public, so
reference:
- `widget: encode` (first used by `systems/ctf/`): `mode: send` writes `message:` as plain text, binary, hex, base64
    and Encrypted (a key-word Vigenère; input "Key word"), Send buttons "Send as Hex", and Eve tries every public
    decoder; `shared:` is Ava's key word. Values f (0 plain to 4 encrypted), e (Eve can read it), l, q (key matches
    shared), s. `mode: decode` undoes `data:` one layer per button ("Decode as Base64", "Decode with the key word", Undo);
    `plain:` gives d = 1 on a match (leave it out for flags). Values d, u, w, r. `#` can't appear in data (it starts a
    comment).

Encoding is not encryption. A message written as binary, hex or base64 looks scrambled, but the rule is public, so
anyone can turn it back. Encryption needs a secret key as well. Eve, listening on the network, tries every public
decoder on whatever is sent. All of it is pretend: nothing is sent anywhere.
  widget: encode
  mode: send (default) | decode
mode: send
  message: meet at 4                  the starting message (the student can type another; input labelled "Message")
  key: gears                          the starting key word for Encrypted (input labelled "Key word"; letters only)
  shared: gears                       the key word Ava has (q = 1 when the key word matches it)
  Buttons choose what is sent: Plain text, Binary, Hex, Base64 or Encrypted (labelled "Send as Hex"…). Eve's panel
  shows what she can read.
  Values: f (sent as: 0 plain, 1 binary, 2 hex, 3 base64, 4 encrypted), e (1 when Eve can read it), l (message
          length), q (1 when the key word is the shared one), s (messages sent)
mode: decode
  data: 57 50 7b 68 69 7d             the coded data (or the student pastes some: input labelled "Coded data")
  plain: WP{hi}                       optional: the original, for d (leave it out when it is a flag)
  Buttons: Binary, Hex, Base64, Key word (labelled "Decode as Hex"…) turn the current text back one layer; Undo and
  Start again. The key word decoder uses the "Key word" input.
  Values: d (1 when the text is back to plain:), u (decoders that worked), w (decoders that failed), r (1 when the
          text is readable: printable letters with no coding left that a decoder can undo)
The toy cipher (Encrypted, Key word) shifts each printable character by the letters of the key word in turn, a
Vigenère cipher. Real encryption (AES, behind HTTPS) works with keys far too long to guess; the teacher notes say so.
example:
widget: encode
message: meet at the lab at 4
shared: gears

title: Evaporation
description: Recover dissolved salt by evaporating the water.
reference:
A lesson with `language: science` (see `content/science/chemistry/`) is a short concept tutorial for introducing or
revising one idea, beside practical work, never instead of it. One tutorial per hinge node of the XY Model node files
(waypoints-kit `data/science/`); nodes whose response mode is `integration` are left to class tasks.

- **Woven strands.** Human endeavour and Inquiry have no tutorials of their own; they are woven into lessons. A lesson
  lists the ones a student genuinely practises in it as `woven: [AC9S7H03, AC9S7I05]` (descriptor codes from
  `data/curriculum/science.json`; validate checks each is in a woven strand), and the curriculum map lists those lessons on
  the descriptor's card. A predict step alone isn't Inquiry; tag only where the student does the thing (judges a claim,
  finds an anomaly, weighs impacts). Where a descriptor has no lesson, add a short `tier: typical` Elaborate step.
- **5E on the existing stages.** Science pages label the stages in 5E words, so predict-and-compare, decks and
  worksheets work unchanged: `predict` = **Engage** (one `predict` check, with `actual:`), `run` = **Explore** (a board;
  the compare box shows the prediction), `investigate` = **Explain**, `practise` = **Practise** (when the node's response
  mode is consolidation), `modify` = **Elaborate**, `info` = **Evaluate** (a `reflect` check and a revision summary).
- **`prompt:`** (step field; the Learning with AI courses): a copyable AI prompt card, text or `{ title, text }`. The page adds a Copy button and "Use an AI tool your school allows, and only if your teacher says you can". Keep the lesson doable without it (put it on an optional step), one prompt per step, and ask students to check the reply with the habit the lesson practised. General lessons keep coach prompts on recap pages only.
- **`video:`** (step field): a video hosted elsewhere, an `https://` address or `{ url, caption }`. YouTube and Vimeo links become a privacy-friendly embed, `.mp4`/`.webm` files a player, anything else a link. For teacher-made lessons (Create's student links); site lessons use recorded clips.
- **Width tiers** (any lesson, not only science): `tier: typical` or `tier: wider` on a step marks extra contexts beyond
  the minimum path. The page shows a Minimum / Typical / Wider control; `?width=` in the link sets the floor (a
  teacher's choice), students can widen but not narrow, and the default is typical. Tiered steps' checks are not
  needed to finish the lesson and are left out of course progress. Worksheets wrap them in `:::typical` / `:::wider`.
  Wider means more contexts, never harder content.
- **`sort` check, sort into groups** (any lesson; not ordering, which is `parsons`): `options:` are groups, `items:` are `[text, group]` or `[text, group, why]`; a group can
  be used many times (unlike `match`), and extra groups act as distractors. The why shows once an item is right.
- **`question` feedback** (any lesson): `feedback:` is one entry per option (text, or `null`), shown when that wrong
  option is chosen. Aim each at the misconception behind the option.
- **`board` check:** `expect: { done: true }` ticks when the science board's widget finishes its task.
- **The science board** (`playground-science/`: `engine.js` is the particle engine, `main.js` the widgets; JSXGraph).

  `bench`, `filter`, `evaporate`, `distil`, `chroma`, `box` (a model to look at), `windows` (`set: floatsink | six |
  ice | abc`, static diagrams) and `quiz` (`need:`, `options: Label=value; …`, repeated `item: text | value | why`).
  Each task's `starter` loads its own board. Nothing on the board is saved.
- **Atoms and reactions** (`atoms.js`, for Years 8–10 chemistry): molecules built from element atoms (model-kit
  colours, symbols on by default, `labels: off` hides them), moving as a gas in a box shaped to the screen with the same
  area everywhere. Particles are written `H2 x4` or `4 H2`; formulas use real element symbols (a typo is an error).
  - `widget: atoms`, `show: H2 x4, O2 x3, H2O x5`, optional `need:` (kinds to inspect; default all) and `temp:` (K).
    Students click particles (or press Inspect next particle) to see each kind's atoms, element or compound; with
    more than one kind the board names the box a mixture. Done once `need` kinds are inspected.
  - `widget: reaction`, `show:` and one or more `react: H2 + Cl2 -> 2 HCl` lines (atoms must balance, or the board
    refuses). Options: `ea:` energy a collision needs, in multiples of the average energy (default 3); `release:`
    energy given out per reaction (negative absorbs; try 0.5–1); `temp:` (default 300 K) and `temps: 150-600` for the
    slider (`slider: off` hides it); `catalyst: on` (a toggle that halves `ea`); `hold: on | off` (keep the temperature
    fixed; default on unless `release` is set, so exothermic and endothermic reactions warm or cool the gas);
    `target: HCl 10` (default: three quarters of what the first reaction can make). `goal:` is `target` (done when the
    target is reached), `react` (done at the first reaction), `compare` (done after reaching the target under two
    different conditions; a run whose temperature or catalyst changed part-way does not count) or `none`.
    The panel shows counts, the atom tally before and now, collisions and reactions, temperature and time; a yellow
    ring marks each collision that reacts. Simplifications to name for students: 2D, rigid molecules, and reactions with
    more than two reactants (CH4 + 2 O2) take the extra particles from nearby rather than in several steps.
    With about ten of each reactant, run times vary by a factor of two or so: use 15 or more for rate comparisons.
- **Cooling magma** (`crystals.js`, 8U04 node 2): `widget: cooling`. Students pick a cooling speed (Very slow, Slow,
  Fast, Very fast, Instant: each names where it happens, from deep underground to lava quenched in seconds), press
  Cool the magma and watch crystals start and grow; each finished run adds a row (crystals, average and largest size,

  worksheets work unchanged: `predict` = **Engage** (one `predict` check, with `actual:`), `run` = **Explore** (a board;
  the compare box shows the prediction), `investigate` = **Explain**, `practise` = **Practise** (when the node's response
  mode is consolidation), `modify` = **Elaborate**, `info` = **Evaluate** (a `reflect` check and a revision summary).
- **`prompt:`** (step field; the Learning with AI courses): a copyable AI prompt card, text or `{ title, text }`. The page adds a Copy button and "Use an AI tool your school allows, and only if your teacher says you can". Keep the lesson doable without it (put it on an optional step), one prompt per step, and ask students to check the reply with the habit the lesson practised. General lessons keep coach prompts on recap pages only.
- **`video:`** (step field): a video hosted elsewhere, an `https://` address or `{ url, caption }`. YouTube and Vimeo links become a privacy-friendly embed, `.mp4`/`.webm` files a player, anything else a link. For teacher-made lessons (Create's student links); site lessons use recorded clips.
- **Width tiers** (any lesson, not only science): `tier: typical` or `tier: wider` on a step marks extra contexts beyond
  the minimum path. The page shows a Minimum / Typical / Wider control; `?width=` in the link sets the floor (a
  teacher's choice), students can widen but not narrow, and the default is typical. Tiered steps' checks are not
  needed to finish the lesson and are left out of course progress. Worksheets wrap them in `:::typical` / `:::wider`.
  Wider means more contexts, never harder content.
- **`sort` check, sort into groups** (any lesson; not ordering, which is `parsons`): `options:` are groups, `items:` are `[text, group]` or `[text, group, why]`; a group can
  be used many times (unlike `match`), and extra groups act as distractors. The why shows once an item is right.
- **`question` feedback** (any lesson): `feedback:` is one entry per option (text, or `null`), shown when that wrong
  option is chosen. Aim each at the misconception behind the option.
